content.text: Events are powerful for modding and easy to learn.
When writing an event (or event chain) the steps are usually the following:

items.text: Decide for whom the event should fire. There are often multiple ways to script an event chain, but some are more efficient/simpler!
Decide if the event should trigger by itself or be triggered by something else ( on action , decision , or other event).
If it triggers by itself, use fast triggers to prevent the trigger from being evaluated for EVERY single character in the world, which costs a lot of computer power.

content.text: Once you've finished scripting, usually you'll need to:

items.text: Run The Validator to make sure there are no syntax errors (it's way faster to catch error this way, as testing in-game is not very efficient.)
Load the game, and use console commands to meet the conditions of the event (can be seen via testevent <EventID> <CharOrProvID> )
Manually fire the event via event <EventID> <CharOrProvID> , to check there are no design errors and verify localizations.

content.text: Events usually consist of:

items.text: an initial trigger which fires the event on a character
a "mean time to happen"; or average time it takes for the event to fire
one or more options which will affect the character in the event-writer's chosen way

content.text: There are several types of events:

rows: Basic character event. Vanilla frames: GFX_event_normal_frame_diplomacy, GFX_event_normal_frame_war, GFX_event_normal_frame_economy, GFX_event_normal_frame_intrigue, GFX_event_normal_frame_religion

Bigger popup for character events, used in vanilla learning scenario. Vanilla frames: GFX_event_long_frame_diplomacy, GFX_event_long_frame_war, GFX_event_long_frame_economy, GFX_event_long_frame_intrigue, GFX_event_long_frame_religion.

Shows the sender in-game. Vanilla frames: GFX_event_letter_frame_diplomacy, GFX_event_letter_frame_war, GFX_event_letter_frame_war_big, GFX_event_letter_frame_economy, GFX_event_letter_frame_intrigue, GFX_event_letter_frame_religion.

Similar to character_event, but with a large ornamented first letter, fancy frame, and slightly larger window. Vanilla frames: GFX_event_narrative_frame_diplomacy, GFX_event_narrative_frame_war, GFX_event_narrative_frame_economy, GFX_event_narrative_frame_intrigue, GFX_event_narrative_frame_religion.

Basic province event. Warning: Fires to the owner of the province, but ROOT is the province. If the province has no owner (eg. wasteland/ocean), then the event will not fire. Vanilla frames: same as character_event.

Used for notifications to diplomatic decisions, such as Declare War or Revoke Title. Can only be fired via on_action events. FROM is the character receiving the event, FROMFROM is the person sending the event. ROOT is empty or a third party, new_character is empty or a third party. Vanilla frames: same as letter_event if associated with hardcoded decisions. Window is hidden otherwise.

Used to unlock "Viking Raider" achievement. Can only be fired via on_action events. Warning: ROOT is the unit only when the event is fired via on_entering_port. Otherwise it's the owner. Vanilla frames: same as character_event.
Allow to define a quest_target that is determined in the immediate block of the event. For instance quest_target = event_target:infiltration_target

content.text:
Event IDs must be unique, as event collisions can result in bugs and CTDs.
To improve compatibility between mods , and reduce the chance of identical IDs, namespaces can (and should!) be used.

Namespaces can be any alphanumeric string (without the '.' character), and are used as prefix in the form <namespace>.<id> .
If an event file uses a namespace, it has to be declared at the beginning of the file with namespace = <namespace> . This has to be done for every file the namespace is used in.

At load time, namespaces are resolved to a numeric value. For instance event <namespace>.3132 may be transformed into ID 1403132 (i.e. <namespace> is 1,400,000 or 14).
Because of this:

items.text: event IDs without a namespace must not go over 999,999
event IDs with a namespace must not go over 99,999

content.text: Below is an example of the use of the namespace "mymod":

Note that neither the "EVTDESC" nor "EVTOPT" prefix are required—nor do the localisation keys even technically need to be related to your namespace at all—but it is best practice by far to choose a clear and clash-free naming convention based on your mod.  Provided the localisation keys exist, the above example would work just as successfully as:

where mymodprefix is a unique prefix you've chosen to distinguish your mod.  If you choose to do this, of course, be careful to use prefixes that do not clash with jargon —nothing would be more embarrassing than choosing a key like "cb_" for your hypothetical mod Crusader Babes, only to find that you are overwriting numerous casus belli keys from the base game.  (Nothing more embarrassing, perhaps, with the exception of making the mod in the first place.)
Descriptions define the text of the event and can either be a fixed localization key or a dynamic block.  A fixed localisation key is simply expressed in the form desc = key :
A dynamic block is similar but includes a series of trigger conditions that determine whether a description will appear

If multiple descriptions can appear according to their trigger conditions, a list of all available descriptions will be generated and one of the descriptions will be chosen randomly by the game engine.  This can also be done with static localisation keys.  For instance:
This will randomly display one of the four descriptions provided when the event is triggered.  (This feature also works for option descriptions.)

Event pictures are the horizontal pictures that appear on the top of an event scroll. Like descriptions they can either be fixed event_pictures or a dynamic block.  A fixed localisation key is simply expressed in the form picture = key , for example:

A dynamic block is similar but includes a series of trigger conditions that determine whether the listed picture will be replaced. Note that the picture has to be defined under the dynamic description block, this is true even if the description is the same throughout with only the picture changing.

Since 3.0, you can also have triggers on the pictures themselves, allowing you to define multiple pictures without having to go via event descriptions. Note that event description pictures will still take precedence.
Keep in mind that these triggers are resolved after the immediate command block has been run, which you need to take into account if you're using conditionals that get changed in the same event.

It should be noted that the name used to call an event picture is not always the same as the name for the event picture. In the example above: GFX_evt_battle_byzantine doesn't call a file named battle_byzantine, instead it calls the file Battle_Cataphracts_Saracen. This is because in order to call an event picture the event picture needs to be defined in a gfx file in the interface folder, and sometimes the call name differs from the file name. If a call name does not match any text from the gfx file in the interface folder, your event will have the default event picture.

In addition, many event pictures and their defining files are not located in the main event_pictures and interface folders. These are instead found in their corresponding dlc zip folder. For example: the event pictures for the Sunset Invasion DLC and their defining gfx file are located in the dlc/dlc018.zip folder.

You can also create your own event picture. To do so, make the picture a 450 x 150 .dds or .tga file inside of the gfx/event_pictures folder. Then define the file inside of a gfx file inside of the interface folder like so;
The name calls it and the texture file points to the needed file. You can make name anything you want, but usually it is best to set it to be the same as the file name for simplicity.

Used with window . Specifies the background of the event and will also apply that GFX name + "_option" to the option buttons if GFX by that name exists.

Image that shows up at the top of the event (450x150 px). Not needed in case of hide_window = yes, nor for letter_event. References an entry in interface/*.gfx folder (ex: GFX_evt_council). Those entries can be overridden by culture and/or religion by defining a gfx entry GFX_<picture>_<religion> or GFX_<picture>_<culture>.
Frame for the popup. Event types have different matching frames.

Determines which character is shown in the upper-right corner in a character_event , long_character_event , province_event , narrative_event , or the sole portrait in a letter_event . For an offmap power, will show the ruler of the offmap. Won't show anything if hide_from = yes is used. portrait = none is an alternative to hide_from = yes .

Used for some vanilla tutorial events. These are referenced in NLearningScenario section of defines .

Usually used in combination with major = yes

If notification = yes then the event will be displayed according to the player's "Notification Events" choice in "Message Settings". Note: Not very nice for province_event , as it will show an empty character portrait in the notification. Not useful for events with any meaningful options (as players will not be able to click an option if the event is relegated to the high-priority/low-priority/log window). Not useful for events which the player must see, because they may have disabled notification events in their message settings, and there's no way to know if they have done so. "Notification Events" can be found by going into "Message Settings" and scrolling about 4/5 of the way down the "All" list. Counterintuitively, notifications for events where ROOT is the player character are controlled by the "other characters of message interest" setting ( not "you or close and unlanded family members").

content.text: Pre-triggers or fast triggers are special conditions at the root of events, that allow the engine to filter potentially eligible events for a character, without having to evaluate the trigger block. [1] [2]
There’s no limit to how many pre-triggers, other than there only being one of each (except for DLC checks).
Most pre-triggers only work for character events, but a few can also be used in province events as of patch 2.6 .
Warning: some pre-triggers have a different name than the equivalent normal condition!

Few pre-triggers are significantly more effective, because they’re kept in separate event lists that are only ever evaluated if a character meets their condition. These can be considered "filtering" pre-triggers since they can completely eliminate events from even preliminary evaluation.
They are, in order of precedence:

rows: If yes, will only fire for ai characters. If no, will only fire for the player(s). Implies only_playable = yes .
Checks if a character owns a family palace. Implies only_playable = yes .
Excludes vassals and tributaries. Implies only_playable = yes .

In script, "playable" means: count-tier or above, or a patrician, and is not a landless rebel, even if of an unplayable government. Using this pre-trigger completely eliminates evaluation of the event for anyone who does not meet the criteria, meaning that the event is checked for the ~1000 playable characters in the game, rather than all ~20k

Restricts to characters that are backing or leading a plot. Takes precedence over everything except only_playable (as well as anything that implies only_playable ), as the number of characters involved in plots is generally lower than the number of rulers.
Excludes untitled characters. This is a lesser version of only_playable , as it includes barons, rebels, etc. (i.e. anyone holding any landed title).

Restricts the event for members of the religion/religion_group. It is mutually exclusive with the other filtering pre-triggers, i.e only_playable (as well as anything that implies only_playable ) and only_rulers both take precedence, so in some cases it might actually be better to just use religion_group = SOME_RARE_GROUP and leave out only_rulers = yes .

Restricts the event for members of the religion/religion_group. It is mutually exclusive with the other filtering pre-triggers, i.e only_playable (as well as anything that implies only_playable ) and only_rulers both take precedence, so in some cases it might actually be better to just use religion_group = SOME_RARE_GROUP and leave out only_rulers = yes .

items.text: If yes, will only fire for ai characters.
If no, will only fire for the player(s). Implies only_playable = yes .

content.text: Other pre-triggers are simply checked at the start of event evaluation, which is slightly quicker than checking them in the trigger itself. All are cheap checks and so should be used as much as possible (but are not worth contorting the logic of events to make them work).

rows: Minimum age of the character (for this event).
Maximum age of the character (for this event).

Will never ever get evaluated if DLC is enabled/disabled by the player (or in the case of multiplayer, the host). Can be applied more than once per event, to filter based on many DLCs.

Example: in_command = no will make the event only trigger for people not commanding troops (since patch 3.0 ). Warning: not tested, seems to be buggy right now

content.text: The trigger of an event is responsible for making sure the event is fired at the proper time on the proper character. There are many different conditions which can be used under 'trigger'. They all serve the purpose of adding flavor to the game. In some instances events may have the line: is_triggered_only = yes , this means that the event is triggered by the option of another event, therefore it will not fire unless the option in question is chosen by the character.

All events (except those with is_triggered_only = yes ) need a trigger section. This defines when the event can trigger, and is where much of the power of event modding lies. Here you can check almost any condition, the only limit is the scopes and conditions you have available, and your creativity.
Below is an example trigger section:

Mean time to happen (MTTH) is a measure of how much time it takes, on average, for a random event to occur. An MTTH of 90 days, for example, means that after 90 days, the probability of the event having been fired is exactly 50%.  The use of the "mean time to happen" value rather than probability allows modders and developers to specify how often they feel an event should occur, independent of the mechanics that make events fire. Thus, it removes the need for calculating probabilities while coding.

Like with the trigger, mean_time_to_happen has to be defined for any event that isn't is_triggered_only = yes . This section determines the average time it takes for an event to happen. This is typically defined in months, but can also be defined in days or years. 
It can be affected by modifiers depending on virtually any condition .
Below is an example section:

Weight multiplier is an alternative to mean-time-to-happen required by on_action events, introduced in patch 2.0 .  It is more efficient to handle by the engine and much faster than using events with a very low mean-time-to-happen to poll for changes.  Events called by on_actions must use weight_multiplier instead of mean_time_to_happen .  Although the engine does also support the use of weight multipliers for regular events instead of MTTH, it is not recommended for events with a low delay as they will queue up and then fire once per month in a large batch of popups. The Validator will report all such uses as an error.
Weight multiplier modifiers, as used by on_action events , increase the chance of an event occurring, rather than increase the amount of time the event takes.
For example, this is an event in the game where the factors increase the chance of the event occurring, rather than increasing the amount of time the event takes:
Commands in the immediate = { } block are executed before the event is displayed (i.e even before description and title localization gets resolved).

Warning: when firing an event with no delay within immediate block, the new event actually uses the original event's scope (sort of like a sub-routine), rather than creating a copy of these scopes. This can lead to unexpected effects when used with event targets [4]
Commands in the after = { } block are executed after an option is selected and run, regardless of which option is chosen.

Commands in the fail_trigger_effect = { } block are executed if script attempts to trigger an event, but the trigger isn't fulfilled. Useful for handling things like one character in a chain dying for unrelated reasons partway through the chain.

Finally, every event (with the exception of events with the hide_window = yes tag) needs one or more (maximum 4 eligible) option section. Once an option is selected, the associated effects will be applied.

The options listed in an event are arguably one of the most crucial parts of the event itself. They allow the player to decide upon which option best suites their current needs or wants, as well as occasionally forcing the character to choose an option depending on their traits and/or attributes .
The only requirement for an option is a name, but you'll typically want to define effects, as well as possibly a trigger which determines when the option shows up. Below is an example option section.
The option name can be a set localisation key or be dynamic, based on meeting certain conditions
In order to help the AI choose the most rational option, ai_chance modifiers can be used.
Each option is weighted based on a base factor, that can be influenced by modifiers, and the chosen option is picked via a weighted random.
For province_events :

items.text: The AI taking the decision is not ROOT , so it is not obvious what syntax should be used inside ai_chance modifier blocks. So far, the following valid formats have been discovered [5] :

children.text: Use province owner conditions by wrapping the conditions in an owner = {...} block. (Eg: modifier = { factor = 0 owner = { trait = gregarious } } is valid.)
Use province owner conditions without any owner = {...} block. (Eg: modifier = { factor = 0 trait = gregarious } is also valid.)

items.text: In particular, it seems to be impossible to use conditions that check the province itself. (Eg: Both of the following are invalid : modifier = { factor = 0 has_province_modifier = prosperity_modifier_1 } ; and modifier = { factor = 0 ROOT = { has_province_modifier = prosperity_modifier_1 } } .)

content.text: Effects that visibly affect single characters will automatically display their portraits on the event option button.

children.text: Effects inside a hidden_tooltip block will not cause an automatic portrait.
Effects that do not produce a tooltip (eg. save_event_target_as ) will often cause an automatic portrait.
Effects inside an any_ scope often do not cause automatic portraits.

items.text: NB: It is impractical to verify these limitations for every possible combination of scope and effect, so you will need to perform targeted testing for your own specific scenario.

content.text: The show_portrait command can be used to force any other character's portrait to be shown in an event option.
The order of event option portraits is unpredictable, and seemingly cannot be influenced in any way.

items.text: They are not ordered by ID number, or by any other obvious criteria.
The order seems to be repeatable, if the same exact set of portraits needs to be displayed.
Reordering show_portrait commands has no impact on the order of portraits.
Reordering single-target effects has no impact on the order of portraits.
Any character whose portrait is shown in the top-left (usually ROOT ) or top-right (usually FROM ) can never be shown in any of that event's options.
At most 10 character portraits can be shown per event option.

children.text: If there are more than 10 show_portrait commands in an event option, then no portraits will be shown .
If more than 10 characters qualify, for some combination of reasons, then only 10 will be shown (but it's impossible to predict which 10, due to the idiosyncratic ordering "feature" described above).

items.text: If an effect in the immediate or after block causes an automatic portrait, that portrait will be shown in every event option, regardless of relevance.

children.text: Workaround: Ensure that the immediate and after blocks contain no visible single-target effects - either by wrapping them in a hidden_tooltip , or by moving them to another (hidden) event.

sections.heading: Option availability hint and border color

content.text: Optionally, an option can specify a border color and a tooltip like "This option is available because...", similar to the events which are available because your character has a special trait.

items.text: tooltip_info = yes : yellow border, no tooltip
tooltip_info_custom = <loc_key> : yellow border and custom tooltip

content.text: Traits added or removed in the option have their icons shown. To show additional trait icons (e.g. ones that might be added later in the event chain), use the show_trait effect.

Events with hide_window = yes can be used to get a specific character into the FROM scope (and the character portrait is, by default, the FROM character). 
So, by sending an event with hide_window = yes to the character you wish to be in the FROM scope (character A), and have that event's option send another event back to the original character B (which would be the FROM of the ping event), you can get A into the FROM scope for B's event. A can now be referenced in localisation and the event code. 
This can be useful:

items.text: when you are using any_ or random_ scopes and need to reference the any_ or random_ character in localisation. See the example code below
when you want to re-use an event chain, but have it triggered from different sources (for instance: MTTH, decision and on_action)

when you want to hide portraits in your event's options. Replace the character scope with a character_event command, then put the original character scope in that new event that pings back. Often used for times when you don't want the player to know which character is getting pinged (e.g. a murder mystery event chain).

content.text:
Events have a maximum of 4 options at one time, but the 4th option of an event can call another event that has more options, allowing more than 4 options.
The last option needs to cycle back to the 1st option.

repeat_event command with the current event ID can be used to fire an event recursively, with a delay.
It fires in the specified scope as ROOT, but does not add a FROM to the stack, thus greatly reducing the risk of stack overflow in case of recursions.

sections.heading: Turn by turn interactive event chains

content.text: Some restrictions apply when an event chain:

items.text: must be playable on both sides by 1 player (the chain can be initiated by the player OR the AI)
interacts between 2 (or more) players in a multiplayer game

content.text: For instance this would apply for an interactive duel by combat, a dice poker mini-game , etc.
The idea is that the result of any action taken by player A must be notified to player B, based on which B takes an action, which is notified to A, etc.

There is a single event chain that alternates between A and B in turns, until the chain reaches an exit condition (for instance a variable counting the number of turns).
To reduce the scripting duplication, events may be designed to be re-used for both A and B, if the opponent is always kept into FROM scope (you don't know if ROOT is player A or player B).
Example of interactive loop (not showing the startup and conclusion events):
Events can be attached to on_action triggers that fire when hardcoded conditions are met. For instance on_marriage fires when two characters marry each other.

This allows to script events that need to happen instantly, and that would otherwise be impossible or very costly to trigger via normal mean-time-to-happen events.
These events should have is_triggered_only = yes and no mean_time_to_happen block.
Note that the fast-triggers and the trigger block of these events will still be checked.

On_action event IDs are referenced by adding a new .txt file in common\on_actions folder (vanilla uses 00_on_actions.txt). 
There are 3 lists:

items.text: Effects that are executed before any events are fired. Use scripted effects if there's any complex logic involved so as to not bloat the on_actions file.

Events that randomly fire based on specified default probability, modified by the weight_multiplier of the event. Within this list there can be different named blocks containing events. Only one event per block will be fired, if any. Blocks with the same name in the same on action in different files are merged.

content.text: The events and effects fire for the ROOT of the on_action.

The following code example will, for ROOT: execute effect1 before any events are fired; fire event1; fire event2; either fire event3 (50% chance), fire event2 (25% chance) or do nothing (25% chance); and, after 5 days, either fire event5 (50% chance) or do nothing (50% chance):

The date when the time based pulses fire for a specific character seem to be dependent on the <Character ID> of the character the pulse fires for and the <Year> the pulse fires in.
These seem to be the respective formulas:
Where day: 1, month: 1 means 1st of January; day: 5, month: 2 means 5th of February; day: 28, month: 11 means 28th of November and so on.
If there is no father or mother, use <Character ID of father> = 0 and/or <Character ID of mother> = 0 respectively.
Note that "on_yearly_childhood_pulse" fires only for characters within a certain age-range (cf. Crusader Kings II/common/on_actions/00_on_actions.txt )
The years in which the non-yearly pulses fire seem to be determined by the following rules:

That means for "on_bi_yearly_pulse" the difference between the <Character ID> and the <Year> needs to be divisible by 2, for "on_five_yearly_pulse" the difference between the <Character ID> and the <Year> needs to be divisible by 5, and for "on_decade_pulse"  the difference between the <Character ID> and the <Year> needs to be divisible by 10.
<childhood_pulse_age> is 6, 8 and 10, i.e the on_childhood_pulse happens when the character is at the age of 6, then when they are at the age of 8, and then again when they are at the age of 10.
<adolescence_pulse_age> is 12 and 14, i.e the on_adolescence_pulse happens when the character is at the age of 12, and again when they are at the age of 14

H is the Heaviside step function defined here as H ( x ) = { 1 , if x > 0 0 , if x ≤ 0 {\displaystyle H(x)={\begin{cases}1,&{\text{if }}x>0\\0,&{\text{if }}x\leq 0\end{cases}}} . It effectively pushes the year of on_childhood_pulse and on_adolescence_pulse to the beginning of next year if the birthday is later than June.

sections.heading: Ensuring your events work as intended in multiplayer

content.text: In multiplayer, for human-controlled characters:

items.text: Events remain on-screen while the game continues to run in the background, for several in-game months.
At the end of this timeout period, the game automatically selects the first visible option.

children.text: Specifically: Any effects in that option are executed, followed by any effects in the after block.

content.text: AI-controlled characters will resolve events "instantly", same as in single-player.

The main implication of this behaviour is that you cannot assume that the game is paused while an event is on-screen . Instead, you have to think about what might change between the event appearing and a player clicking a button. For example:

items.text: One or more of the characters referenced by the event might die (low health, disease, duel, etc).
A title or settlement referenced by the event might change ownership (or be destroyed).
The character may no longer be able to pay a cost.
An interaction may become impossible because of something the AI/player does (eg. marriage, move to a different court, imprisonment)
An event chain that's tied to particular months (eg. base game hunts/feasts/fairs) can end surprisingly "early" (without seeing everything in the chain) if an event is left on-screen by a player.

sections.heading: Structuring events and event chains to avoid these issues

content.text: Ensure that the first visible option is always "the best".

items.text: Since this is the option that will be chosen if the event times-out for any reason (eg. if the player is AFK).
At the very least, ensure that the first visible option is "not bad" (ie. the player's game won't be ruined by being AFK).

content.text: Use the fact that, if you ask the game to do something impossible, then it will just do nothing

items.text: Eg: If you try to imprison someone who's already in someone else's prison, nothing happens.
This can allow you to simplify your logic significantly - you don't need to manually handle every possible error condition.

content.text: For notification events, consider doing the action before notifying the player.

items.text: If something has happened and the player has no meaningful choices which could have changed it, it may be worthwhile to apply the effect before the event becomes visible to the player.
You can do this either via the immediate block in the visible event, or via a hidden event which fires before the visible event.

children.text: Eg: If "all levies in province X vanish", apply the changes to the province, then show an event notifying the province owner.

items.text: If you do this, you should ensure the notification event properly describes what just happened.

children.text: Eg: In words in the description or option text
Eg: Via custom_tooltip commands in the option or after block

items.text: However, you should use this approach with caution because, for some major events (eg. player being assassinated), it is reasonable for players to take a few in-game weeks to ensure the consequences aren't game-ruining (eg. sort out their succession).

content.text: Consider triggering events without waiting for prior events to be resolved

items.text: Eg: Instead of triggering the next event 1 month after an option is chosen, set up a hidden monthly carousel which triggers a new random event every month.

This won't work in every case (eg: you need to know whether acrobats were hired before showing their performance at the feast), but it can help to prevent event chains from accidentally stretching across multiple years.

content.text: Consider calculating costs before showing the event

items.text: In some rare cases, it may be possible for a player to artificially lower a cost by "doing something" while the game is running and the event is  on-screen.
In even rarer cases, this might be important enough that you want to prevent it.

children.text: Calculating the cost beforehand (preferably before the player knows that an event chain has started)
Storing the cost in a variable
Showing the event, using the stored cost instead of a simple command (eg. wealth = mynamespace_evt101_cost instead of scaled_wealth = -1 )

content.text: When considering in-game delays and timeouts, the likely game speed is important:

items.text: How long will the event be visible on-screen?
How long will the player have to react before the next event in the chain occurs?

content.text: Most multiplayer games aim for either speed 2 or speed 3, with minimal player pauses.

items.text: Speed 1 is usually considered a last-resort (it feels very slow)
Speed 2 is a good compromise between steady progress and ability to handle in-game situations easily
Speed 3 allows rapid progress, but it requires constant focus, and complex situations may feel overwhelming
Speed 4 is almost unplayable without pauses (everything happens too fast)
Speed 5 is probably impossible to sustain in multiplayer

content.text: The speed setting decides the minimum duration of an in-game day. However, the actual duration will often be longer then this (due to CPU load, network traffic, etc). The exact minimum values don't seem to have ever been documented by the developers; however, the following approximations seem fairly accurate:
Example:

items.text: You wish to allow at least 1 minute for player reactions (in case they are briefly AFK, or concentrating on something else, etc)
You assume the worst likely scenario (the game is on speed 3, ie. 0.5s/day)
Then the required in-game delay is approximately 4 months (60s / 0.5s/day = 120 days)
